idiom_name: private members + one mediating accessor, with passkey/attorney-client to narrow who may call it
implementation_notes: The classic guard or proxy object collapses into the class's own access control: the state is private, the only public route to it is a mediating member function that consults the policy before touching it, and the compiler enforces that single-entry property for in-process access. Where the privileged path may be callable by selected collaborators only, the passkey/attorney-client idiom narrows the grant: a token type whose constructor is private to the intended friend controls entry to a constructor or method, instead of a blanket friend declaration that hands out every private member. The classic runtime wrapper is still justified when the mediator must be swappable or when the threat is code the toolchain also compiles: C++ access control is a compile-time property, and casts, pointer arithmetic, macros or a '#define private public' build step bypass it, so anything truly security-critical belongs behind an OS boundary or a runtime check the policy itself owns.
pitfalls: Access control is compile-time and intra-process: reinterpret_cast, pointer arithmetic, macros (#define private public) or a friend overload still reach the members - a genuine security boundary needs an OS mechanism.
friend is all-or-nothing: one collaborator that needs a single privileged call gains every private member, so use the passkey/attorney-client idiom instead of widening friendship.
Returning const Record&, a pointer or a span to internal state hands the caller a reference the mediator cannot revoke; return guarded views or copies that carry their own checks.
mutable members and caches let a const accessor change shared state; if a cache stores a decision, revocation must still update or drop it.
